title: Wait, stream or push
brief: A remote agent's job takes anywhere from two seconds to two days, and your caller may sit behind a firewall, on a phone or in a serverless function. Duration, reachability and update frequency are open. Choose how updates arrive, and learn how bindings and versions affect that choice.

blocks.title: Update delivery in A2A
blocks.intro: The spec offers three complementary mechanisms [[r1]] [[r7]].

options.name: Polling
pros: Simple and works with every binding
cons: Load grows with callers times polling rate
options.bestWhen: Infrequent updates, simple clients or no inbound connectivity.

options.name: Streaming (SSE or native)
options.summary: `SendStreamingMessage` or `SubscribeToTask` delivers events in order as they happen.
pros: Low latency and efficient for frequent updates
Reconnect to a live task with `SubscribeToTask`, whose first event is the current Task
cons: Proxies can buffer or cut streams
options.bestWhen: Interactive apps, dashboards and live progress.
options.avoidWhen: Tasks run for hours or the client cannot hold a connection.

options.name: Push notifications
options.summary: The agent POSTs updates to a webhook the client registered.
cons: The client must be reachable over HTTPS
Adds SSRF, replay and forgery defenses
options.bestWhen: Server-to-server integrations and very long tasks.
options.avoidWhen: Mobile or firewalled clients that cannot receive inbound calls.

blocks.title: Pick a delivery mode
blocks.prompt: Flip task duration, whether the callee can reach you and how much progress you need.

dials.label: Callee can POST to your webhook

options.name: Blocking SendMessage
options.summary: The default: wait for a terminal or interrupted state.

options.name: Stream
options.summary: Hold a connection and receive events.

seconds.why: A short call returns before any timeout.

final.why: One answer is all you need.

seconds.why: Extra round trips for a quick answer.

minutes.why: A modest polling rate is cheap.

no.why: Works behind firewalls and on every binding.

yes.why: Works, though push may be cheaper.

final.why: Fine when you need only the result.

minutes.why: Ideal for live progress while a connection is practical.

days.why: Holding a connection for hours is fragile. Reconnect with `SubscribeToTask`.

no.why: Only the client opens a connection.

progress.why: Events arrive in order as they happen.

seconds.why: Webhook setup for a quick call.

minutes.why: Works, but a stream is often simpler.

days.why: No connection to hold across hours or days.

progress.why: Possible, but each event is a POST.

blocks.takeaway: Duration and reachability decide between a held connection and a webhook. Polling is the baseline that always works.

blocks.title: Push notification flow
blocks.alt: The client sends a message with a push configuration and asks to return immediately. The agent returns a submitted task and later posts status and completion events to the client's webhook, which answers 2xx.
blocks.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant A as Agent
  participant W as Webhook
  C->>A: SendMessage with taskPushNotificationConfig
  A-->>C: Task in SUBMITTED state
  A->>W: POST statusUpdate with credentials
  W-->>A: 2xx
  A->>W: POST task with artifacts on completion
  W-->>A: 2xx
blocks.caption: The push configuration can ride in `SendMessageConfiguration.taskPushNotificationConfig`, with an empty task id, or be created later with the push configuration operations. Payloads use the same `StreamResponse` format as streaming [[r1]].

blocks.title: SendMessage waits by default
blocks.md: `SendMessageConfiguration.returnImmediately` defaults to false. The call then waits until the task reaches a terminal or interrupted state. Set it to true to get the task back at once and then poll, stream or rely on push. The flag has no effect when the agent answers with a direct Message, or for streaming calls. The operation summary in section 3.1.1 phrases the return more loosely than the configuration section, so test your SDK's behavior [[r1]].

blocks.title: Failure modes and how to detect them

items.symptom: The caller hangs for the whole job on `SendMessage`
items.cause: The default blocking mode was used for a long task
items.fix: Set `returnImmediately` to true and poll, stream or use push. Alert on call durations above your timeout budget

items.symptom: A dropped stream loses the result
items.cause: The client treated the stream as the task. Task lifecycle is independent of any stream
items.fix: Reconnect with `SubscribeToTask`, which returns the current Task first so no update is missed, or fall back to `GetTask`

items.symptom: The agent's webhook calls reach internal services
items.cause: Client-supplied webhook URLs were trusted. That is an SSRF and DDoS amplification risk
items.fix: Reject private, loopback and link-local ranges, use allowlists or ownership challenges, and apply egress controls [[r7]]

items.symptom: Duplicate or forged notifications change state
items.cause: The receiver did not verify credentials, task id or freshness
items.fix: Verify credentials, check the task id, reply 2xx, process idempotently and reject stale timestamps or reused ids

items.symptom: A 0.3 client fails to parse replies from a 1.0 agent
items.cause: Enum casing, the `kind` discriminator and operation names changed, and the version was not negotiated
items.fix: Send `A2A-Version` on every request and keep a dual-support phase while clients migrate

blocks.caption: All supported bindings MUST be functionally equivalent [[r1]]
head: Binding
Wire format
Streaming
Notes
rows: REST paths such as `POST /message:send`. `application/a2a+json` SHOULD be used

blocks.md: Service parameters `A2A-Version` and `A2A-Extensions` travel as HTTP headers. Clients choose any binding the card declares and SHOULD fall back to another when one fails. A `tenant` field lets one endpoint host many agents [[r1]].

items: Clients send `A2A-Version: Major.Minor`. An empty header means 0.3, and an unsupported version returns `VersionNotSupportedError`. Patch numbers are never negotiated [[r1]].
Enum values became SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE with prefixes such as `TASK_STATE_` and `ROLE_`. The `kind` discriminator and the `final` flag on status events were removed [[r2]].

Operations were renamed, for example `message/send` to `SendMessage`. `protocolVersion` moved into each interface. `supportsAuthenticatedExtendedCard` became `capabilities.extendedAgentCard`. `ListTasks`, `tenant` and cursor pagination are new [[r2]].
The migration guide suggests three phases: a compatibility layer, dual support, then v1.0 only [[r2]].
The migration page says the implicit and password OAuth flows were removed, while the normative spec still lists them as Deprecated. The spec is authoritative [[r1]] [[r2]].

items.title: Verifying webhooks with JWT and JWKS

items: The client registers `authentication.scheme` of `Bearer` and an optional expected issuer or audience.
The agent signs a JWT with `iss`, `aud`, `iat`, `exp`, `jti` and `taskId`, and publishes its public keys at a JWKS endpoint.
The webhook reads the `kid`, fetches the key (cache it), verifies the signature and validates the claims.
The webhook also checks the `token` from the push configuration, rejects stale timestamps and refuses reused `jti` values [[r7]].

quiz.q: 1,000 callers each poll `GetTask` every 5 seconds while a 3-hour task runs. How many `GetTask` requests per hour does the agent absorb?
quiz.explain: Each caller makes 3,600 divided by 5, or 720, requests per hour. Times 1,000 callers is 720,000 per hour. Push or streaming replaces this constant load with events only when state changes, which is why long tasks favor push.

quiz.q: A caller's `SendMessage` blocks for 40 minutes. The card declares `pushNotifications: true` and the request set no configuration. What explains it?
options: Push notifications must first be activated by a separate administrator call before any message can return a task handle
`returnImmediately` defaults to false, so the call waits for a terminal or interrupted state
The agent is using the gRPC binding, which is always synchronous
A2A forbids tasks longer than 30 minutes
quiz.explain: With the default blocking mode the operation waits until the task is terminal or interrupted. Setting `returnImmediately: true` returns the task at once. Push configuration does not change blocking, gRPC is not synchronous by nature, and the spec sets no task duration limit.

quiz.q: Select every defense that fits A2A push notifications.
options: The agent rejects webhook URLs that point to private, loopback or link-local addresses
The receiver verifies the credentials and that the task id is one it created
The receiver processes notifications idempotently because duplicates can occur
The agent follows redirects to internal hosts so delivery always succeeds
The agent removes timeouts so slow webhooks never fail
quiz.explain: URL validation prevents SSRF, receiver verification prevents forgery, and idempotent handling tolerates retries. Following redirects to internal hosts defeats SSRF controls, and the spec recommends 10 to 30 second timeouts with exponential backoff.

quiz.q: The callee runs 20-minute jobs. Your client sits behind a corporate firewall that blocks inbound calls and needs only the final result. Which delivery mode fits best?
options: Push notifications to a public webhook
A held SSE stream for the full 20 minutes
`SendMessage` with `returnImmediately: true`, then poll `GetTask` at a modest interval
quiz.explain: A firewall blocks webhooks and a 20-minute stream or blocking call is fragile. Returning immediately and polling needs only outbound connectivity, and a modest interval keeps load low when only the final result matters.

takeaways: Polling always works, streaming suits live progress, push suits long tasks and reachable callers.
`SendMessage` waits by default. Set `returnImmediately: true` for a handle.
Webhooks need SSRF, authenticity and replay defenses. Reconnect streams with `SubscribeToTask`.
Send `A2A-Version` on every request and plan dual support when clients move from 0.3 to 1.0.
